corrections.title: Host PreToolUse `skim rewrite` hook collapses a compound command's newlines and prefixes `skim` onto the matched subcommand, corrupting a heredoc-quoted git commit into an exit-127 syntax error
corrections.cause: A compound Bash command containing `git status`, `git log`, `cat <path>` or `head -N <path>` is re-serialised before it runs, with every newline collapsed to a single space and `skim` prefixed onto the matched subcommand. Nothing rejects the command and no static pre-check is involved: the rewritten one-liner is handed to the shell, so a heredoc-quoted `git commit` sharing that line loses the newlines its heredoc needs and dies as `syntax error near unexpected token` at exit 127. The rewriter is a host PreToolUse hook, not the Bash tool and not the orchestrator: ~/.claude/settings.json registers matcher `Bash` -> ~/.claude/hooks/skim-rewrite.sh (skim-hook v2.1.0), which execs `skim rewrite --hook`; reproduced against skim 2.3.1. A command matching none of those targets produces empty hook output and reaches the shell byte-identical, so a bare heredoc `git commit` is NOT affected -- the founding sighting broke only because the same line also carried `git status` and `git log`. The cause is a third-party binary under the operator's ~/.claude and is not fixable in this repository; the agent-facing rule (never put a multi-line construct and a rewrite target in one Bash call) is owned by task 5683.
corrections.note: CORRECTION (task 5686). This entry had NO cause at all, and its title named the rewriter as an unidentified command-rewriting/interception layer; both are replaced with a mechanism REPRODUCED first-hand, which is what legibility census 2026-09-20 listed in its section 4 as unverified (section 1.1 had the discriminator only statistically: 3-of-3 flattened commands carried a git status/log subcommand, 0-of-14 that did not). The reproduction fed `/home/leo/.cargo/bin/skim rewrite --hook` the PreToolUse JSON for this entry's own founding command and got back, on stdout at rc=0, updatedInput.command = `git add -- . && skim git status --short && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF )" && skim git log --oneline -1` -- the corrupted line this entry was filed for, with newlines collapsed to single spaces and `skim` prefixed onto both git subcommands. The same command with the `git status` and `git log` clauses removed returned EMPTY stdout: not rewritten. Reproduced against skim 2.3.1 / skim-hook v2.1.0 at HEAD 854bd3f91b. This ANNOTATES rather than retracts the existing sighting (session fbd7b22b-949a-4047-8087-6a719edb1dc2, 2026-09-19): that observation was true and the symptom real -- only the explanation was missing, which is why every recurrence arrived as a fresh candidate with nothing to match against. Status stays `open`: the defect is live and unfixed, and the corrected cause is what lets the nightly coder match a recurrence onto this entry. Landed through the sole writer scripts/legibility/codebook.py::apply_coding_record; the codebook is never hand-edited.

corrections.title: Compound Bash commands containing a skim-rewrite target (`git status`, `git log`, `cat <path>`, `head -N <path>`) reach the shell with every newline collapsed to a single space, breaking heredocs and inline multi-line scripts
corrections.cause: The discriminator is whether the command ALSO contains `git status`, `git log`, `cat <path>` or `head -N <path>` -- checkable against every sighting here. When one matches, a host PreToolUse hook re-serialises the WHOLE compound command with every newline collapsed to a single space and `skim` prefixed onto the matched subcommand; when none matches the command reaches the shell byte-identical. Nothing is rejected and no static pre-check is involved: the flattened one-liner is handed to the shell, which is why the symptom is an IndentationError from a `python3 -c` script, a `fatal: ambiguous argument` from git, or `syntax error near unexpected token` at exit 127 from a heredoc-quoted commit, rather than a refusal. The chain is ~/.claude/settings.json matcher `Bash` -> ~/.claude/hooks/skim-rewrite.sh (skim-hook v2.1.0) -> `skim rewrite --hook`, reproduced against skim 2.3.1. Two corollaries a reader will otherwise get wrong: the match is on the command WORD, not the text, so a quoted `echo "git status"` does NOT trigger it; and a TOP-LEVEL heredoc redirect (`python3 - <<'PY' ... PY`) makes the hook decline the whole command even when a target IS present -- that is the safe way to pass a multi-line script. The cause is a third-party binary under the operator's ~/.claude and is not fixable in this repository; the agent-facing rule is owned by task 5683.
corrections.note: CORRECTION (task 5686). This entry's prior title -- "Bash tool's static-analysis pre-check rejects multi-line heredoc/multi-command scripts outright, conflating with the 'flattening' bug it was sent to reproduce" -- is WITHDRAWN as refuted on both halves by a direct reproduction: nothing is rejected, and no pre-check is involved. The command is silently re-serialised and handed to the shell. Legibility census 2026-09-20 section 5 already directed this retitle but asked for it to be marked inferred until reproduced; the reproduction under task 5686 is what removes that caveat, so it is now stated as measured. Method: `/home/leo/.cargo/bin/skim rewrite --hook` was fed PreToolUse JSON directly and returned, at rc=0, an updatedInput.command with newlines collapsed to single spaces and `skim` prefixed onto each matched subcommand; commands carrying no target returned EMPTY stdout. Reproduced against skim 2.3.1 / skim-hook v2.1.0 at HEAD 854bd3f91b. This ANNOTATES rather than retracts this entry's existing sightings: each was a true observation of a real symptom, and only the cause they were filed under was refuted. They remain valid evidence and are all consistent with the corrected mechanism -- the flattening they record is real, it is simply not a rejection. Status stays `open`: the defect is live and unfixed, and a correct cause is what lets the nightly coder match recurrences onto this entry instead of filing new candidates.
